Title: #NSTviral: Low-flying helicopter at Pulau Kapas beach sparks criticism
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A helicopter flying low over a beach at Pulau Kapas, Terengganu, has drawn criticism after its rotor wash sent sand and loose items flying among beachgoers.
A video posted on
Threads by @arifwengweng_officiall
showed the helicopter hovering close to the shoreline, at one point appearing to approach the beach as if preparing to land.
The rotor wash kicked up clouds of sand, forcing visitors to shield themselves as food and personal belongings were blown about.
The poster criticised the incident, noting that sand had been blown onto beachgoers and their picnic meals.
The video also drew criticism from other users, some of whom questioned the pilot's actions and called on the Civil Aviation Authority of Malaysia (CAAM) to investigate.
"Can that pilot really try to land in an area crowded with people? Maybe if it was an emergency," user @apau795 said.
Another user, @nohanan, likened the pilot to "a reckless 'mat rempit' who got a helicopter licence."
Meanwhile, @rahimi.ramlee called on CAAM to revoke the pilot's licence and require the pilot to undergo flight training again.
NST has reached out to CAAM for comment.

Title: Berlin police shoot dead chief suspect in deadly Pride parade attack
Article:
BERLIN: German police said Sunday they had shot and killed the chief suspect in what officials described as a deadly Islamist attack near the Berlin Pride parade the previous night, the latest ramming assault to hit the country.
The attack late Saturday – the first such incident to target the German capital's LGBTQ community – killed one woman and wounded 29 others.
Berlin police said on X that they had traced the chief suspect, 21-year old Abdul Ballout, to an allotment complex in the western Spandau district at around 6pm (1600 GMT) on Sunday.
Ballout "ran towards them with a bladed weapon", the police said, prompting officers to open fire, "injuring the suspect so that he died at the scene despite attempts to rescusitate him."
Earlier, prosecutors had said that Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese origin, had been a supporter of the so-called Islamic State group (IS) with several criminal convictions, the latest dating from May.
Saturday's attack shattered what had been a day of celebration for hundreds of thousands attending Christopher Street Day (CSD), one of Europe's largest Pride events.
Politicians in Germany and elsewhere in Europe widely condemned the attack, while the flag at the German Bundestag was lowered to half mast.
Speaking before a memorial service for the victims at Berlin's Marienkirche church, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz appealed to those targeted by the attack to "not let yourselves be intimidated."
SUSPECT'S CRIMINAL PAST
Shortly before 10pm (2000 GMT) on Saturday a white minivan ran into people on the southern edge of central Berlin's Tiergarten park before crashing into a tree.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said Ballout was suspected of having then used a machete to attack more people.
Dobrindt said 29 people were injured, some seriously.
Merz said Sunday evening that none of the victims were any longer in a life-threatening condition.
The attack took place several hundred metres away from the end of the tightly guarded CSD parade route and the event's main stage at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate.
Dobrindt said Ballout had been known to the authorities for a "high number" of previous crimes and for being radicalised.
"Everything we see here indicates that this was an Islamist terror attack," he said.
Prosecutors said Ballout had previous convictions for bodily harm and extortion committed in 2019, and one for robbery in 2020.
They say that in 2024 he shared IS propaganda on Instagram and the following year travelled to Lebanon in order to fight for the militia in Syria.
He was arrested in Lebanon and sentenced to three months' prison.
On his return to Germany in November he was arrested and held until his conviction in May for "preparing a serious act of subversive violence."
But his sentence of one year and ten months in jail was suspended, partially in recognition of the time he had spent in jail in Lebanon and pre-trial detention, and partially because he had admitted to the crimes and distanced himself from IS.
'WON'T BEAT US DOWN'
In a vigil on Sunday afternoon, hundreds of people packed the square in front of the Brandenburg Gate holding rainbow flags and flowers with more gathering nearby.
Luka, a 23-year-old student, told AFP she hoped the attack wouldn't be exploited by the surging anti-immigration far-right ahead of elections in the capital and in several regions in September.
At the scene of the attack itself people left flowers and hand-written messages of condolence and support.
Armin Duenhoelter, 49 from Wolfsburg, who works as a drag artist, was backstage at the main stage when the attack cut short the celebrations.
He told AFP early Sunday that he was still shocked but vowed to be back for next year's CSD.
"We won't let it beat us down," he said.
SPATE OF ATTACKS
Saturday's attack revived memories of a string of similar incidents which have shaken Germany in recent years and inflamed debate on immigration, with several of the perpetrators being from outside Germany.
Martin Hess, a lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), denounced the attack as a result of "a complete failure of the government's security policies."
The deadliest attack in recent years was a truck rampage at a Berlin Christmas market in December 2016 by a Tunisian man with jihadist motives that killed 13 people.
The run-up to last year's general election saw a spate of attacks in public places, including by attackers with Islamist motives.
In 2024, a Saudi psychiatrist and anti-Islam activist killed six people and wounded more than 300 in a car-ramming at a busy Christmas market in the eastern city of Magdeburg.

Title: OGX secures Nokia distributorship for Malaysia
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: OGX Group Bhd's wholly owned subsidiary, OGX Networks Sdn Bhd, has been appointed as an authorised distributor of Nokia's networking infrastructure products and services in Malaysia, expanding the group's enterprise networking portfolio.
OGX Networks has signed a three-year distributorship agreement with Nokia Services and Networks Malaysia Sdn Bhd, with an automatic renewal option thereafter.
The appointment allows OGX Networks to market and distribute Nokia's networking solutions to its system integrator (SI) customers across Malaysia.
Nokia becomes the 19th technology principal within the OGX ecosystem, strengthening the group's offerings in networking infrastructure.
For OGX, the partnership would enhance its ability to support SI partners in meeting growing demand for enterprise, public sector and data centre networking solutions, while creating opportunities for cross-selling, solution integration and deeper channel engagement.
Nokia is a global provider of network infrastructure technologies, with products spanning IP, optical, fixed, data centre and mission-critical connectivity. The company has also been expanding its artificial intelligence-enabled networking capabilities through the integration of AI into data centre fabrics, optical networks and telecommunications infrastructure.
The addition of Nokia Malaysia to OGX's ecosystem would strengthen its ability to deliver high-performance enterprise networking, resilient connectivity infrastructure, data centre interconnectivity, AI-ready network solutions and network modernisation services to customers in Malaysia.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Ringgit opens higher versus US dollar ahead of Negeri Sembilan state poll
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:The ringgit opened higher against the US dollar on Monday, supported by positive domestic sentiment ahead of the Negeri Sembilan state election, an analyst said.
At 8am, the local currency strengthened to 4.0830/0930 against the greenback from 4.0885/0935 at Friday's close.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said market participants would be watching how the state election influences national politics, particularly ahead of polling in Negeri Sembilan.
Early voting for the Negeri Sembilan state election will take place on Tuesday (July 28), with polling scheduled for Aug 1.

Title: Oil slips 5pct after US, Iran pause fighting over weekend
Article:
SINGAPORE: Oil prices tumbled five per cent on Monday after the US and Iran paused strikes over the weekend after two weeks of attacks, raising hopes of a diplomatic solution that would de-escalate the conflict and allow shipping to resume in the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures fell US$4.89, or 5.05 per cent, to US$91.89 by 0009 GMT after briefly slipping under the key support level of US$90 earlier in the session.
US West Texas Intermediate crude was at US$84.64 a barrel, down US$4.67, or 5.23 per cent.
Both contracts are trading at their lowest levels in nearly a week after rising for the past three weeks.
Brent had reached US$100 per barrel as the conflict, which reduced oil shipments via the Strait of Hormuz, spilled over to the Red Sea, hindering exports from the world's top exporter, Saudi Arabia, via the Bab el-Mandeb strait to Asia.
The US ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told "Fox News Sunday" and other US media that President Donald Trump had decided to pause US attacks to allow more time for diplomacy.
"Hopes are rising that a genuine diplomatic path may be opening," IG markets analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note.
"A return to the 14-point MOU (memorandum of understanding) with a little more clarity around control of the Strait of Hormuz would be a solid starting point."
Despite the pause in attacks, fewer than 10 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz daily during the weekend, shipping data from Kpler showed.
In addition, ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb strait fell on Sunday after Yemeni Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast, although a third Chinese supertanker exited via the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
"Any rebound in flows through the Strait of Hormuz is likely to prove slow and partial, as many shippers remain wary and will want greater confidence in their safety before they bring more empty ships into the Strait," MST Marquee analyst Saul Kavonic said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Two teenage girls killed in Teluk Intan crash
Article:
IPOH: Two teenage girls were killed when the motorcycle they were riding was involved in a crash on Jalan Padang Tembak in Teluk Intan yesterday.
Hilir Perak police chief Assistant Commissioner Chua Kok Lian said police received a report on the incident about 6.35pm.
"Preliminary investigations found that the crash is believed to have occurred when a car driven by a 28-year-old man went out of control while attempting to overtake a vehicle in front of it, before colliding with a motorcycle, another car ahead and a young boy by the roadside.
"As a result of the crash, the two teenage girls, who were the rider and pillion of the motorcycle, were pronounced dead at the scene, while the 28-year-old car driver and the young boy were taken to Teluk Intan Hospital for treatment," he said in a statement.
He said the car driver has been detained to assist investigations.
Chua added that police were still investigating the exact cause of the crash.
"Anyone who witnessed the incident or has information related to the crash is urged to come forward to assist in the investigation by contacting investigating officer Inspector Mohd Amirrudin Shafiei at 013-9126959 or by visiting the nearest police station," he said.
The case is being investigated under Section 41(1) of the Road Transport Act 1987 for causing death by reckless or dangerous driving.
Anyone found guilty under the section is liable to a jail term of between two and 10 years and a fine of between RM5,000 and RM20,000.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Asyraf Wajdi urges Education Ministry to follow Mara's army veteran warden initiative
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Education Ministry should consider appointing full-time wardens among army veterans to curb bullying in schools, said Mara chairman Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki.
He said this follows an increasing number of bullying cases reported in schools nationwide.
"Deploying veterans as wardens would provide them with employment opportunities while instilling greater discipline among students," he added.
"Mara is prepared to share with the ministry a study by Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) on the effectiveness of a nine-month pilot project involving full-time external wardens recruited from army veterans at Maktab Rendah Sains Mara (MRSM).
"Among the key findings during the implementation period were zero bullying cases and an increase in student discipline. Monitoring was more consistent, while responses to student welfare and safety issues were faster.
"Additionally, the hostel environment became safer, neater, and more conducive. This positively impacted teachers, who were no longer burdened with warden duties and could focus on their core teaching responsibilities," he said in a Facebook post.
Asyraf Wajdi said academic performance also improved, with highly positive feedback from students during field surveys and visits.
"The combination of firmness and parental values positions these veterans not merely as wardens, but as mentors and educators to the students," he said.
Based on the study, Mara decided to expand the initiative to 10 more MRSM campuses last month as an initial strengthening measure before rolling it out across all 58 MRSM nationwide starting January next year.
"This approach is believed to be capable of strengthening the hostel management system in a more structured, professional, and effective manner.
"I have also asked the UPM team to help develop a dedicated training module for future wardens.
"This module will focus not only on discipline and security, but also on instilling human values, empathy, and parental care, ensuring they truly embrace their role in nurturing MRSM students like parents in a hostel, in line with the Mara Education Philosophy," he said.
He noted that many military personnel end their service between the ages of 38 and 45 and remain in their productive years, making them well-suited for the education sector to help improve student discipline.
"Furthermore, this serves as an alternative solution to address the welfare issues of armed forces veterans, particularly non-pensionable veterans, which are frequently raised.
"They complete their service while still productive, but not all receive a monthly pension, depending on their recognised length of service," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: NS polls: Small group engagements more meaningful than big rallies, says Mat Sabu
Article:
KUALA PILAH: Simple yet meaningful campaign approaches centred on small-group engagements rather than large political rallies allow leaders to connect more personally with voters, says Amanah president Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu.
With just days remaining before polling for the Negri Sembilan election, he said he would continue touring the state to meet residents face-to-face.
"I do not think we need to hold many large ceramah. I prefer gatherings like this where we can meet people and interact with them.
"At big events, we give our speeches, get into our cars and leave. It is a one-way communication.
"Through small-group meetings, we can mingle with the people," he told reporters after attending "Kenduri Sekampung with Mohamad Sabu" in Kampung Ulu Senaling, here.
Also present were Negri Sembilan Amanah chairman Datuk MK Ibrahim Abd Rahman and Senaling candidate Mohd Hanis Mohd Alimin from Pakatan Harapan.
Mohamad, better known as Mat Sabu, said he hoped other coalition leaders would adopt a similar approach during the final stretch of the campaign.
Earlier, he said his visit to Ulu Senaling carried sentimental value as he had lived in Kuala Pilah for two years under a restricted residence order between 1984 and 1986.
He said returning to the area felt like coming home despite many of his old acquaintances having since died.
"Forty years have passed. Many of those I knew are no longer around, but I have been meeting their children and grandchildren.
"It feels like returning to my hometown, and the villagers have given me a very warm welcome," he said.
Mohamad was detained twice under the now-repealed Internal Security Act while serving as an activist with Pas Youth.
He was first detained from 1984 to 1986 on allegations of involvement in extremist activities.
Following his release, he was placed under a restricted residence order in Kuala Pilah for two years. He was detained again under the ISA from 1987 to 1989.
The Kota Raja member of parliament said he also met the former police officer who escorted him from the Bukit Aman lock-up to Kuala Pilah.
He said they have remained on good terms over the years.
"In this struggle, we do not blame people and we should not harbour any resentment.
"The police were carrying out their duties in accordance with the law at that time, and we have maintained a good relationship," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Beyond Property - Why China's Real Economic Challenge Is Household Confidence
Article:
The Crisis Is Not Housing—It Is Confidence
China's greatest economic challenge today is no longer whether it can manufacture more electric vehicles, dominate advanced semiconductors or lead the global race in artificial intelligence. It is whether Chinese households still have the confidence to spend.
China is undergoing its most consequential economic restructuring since Deng Xiaoping launched Reform and Opening-Up in 1978. The challenge is no longer sustaining an investment-led economy, but building a consumption-driven one after property—the country's principal engine of wealth creation—has begun to lose momentum.
For more than three decades, China's rise rested on rapid urbanisation, infrastructure investment and an expanding property market. At its peak, property— including construction and related industries—accounted for an estimated onequarter to one-third of economic activity. Property sales financed local governments through land revenues, while housing became the principal store of household wealth, the dominant form of collateral and the financial foundation of China's expanding middle class. Few major economies have concentrated so much national wealth in a single asset class.
Today those foundations are shifting. Housing prices continue to decline sharply. In many cities they have returned to levels last seen nearly two decades ago, while an estimated 90 million completed or unfinished apartments remain vacant or unsold. Official GDP growth has moderated to around five per cent, compared with the 6–10 per cent expansion that characterised much of China's economic miracle.
A Successful Industrial Pivot
To Beijing's credit, policymakers prevented a systemic financial crisis by redirecting capital away from speculative property towards advanced manufacturing and strategic industries. China is now the world's largest producer of electric vehicles, dominates battery and solar photovoltaic manufacturing, leads in industrial robotics and has emerged as a major force in artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing. These achievements have preserved export competitiveness and kept growth resilient despite the prolonged property correction.
Yet stabilising GDP is not the same as restoring confidence.
Three Balance Sheets Explain China's Transition
China's adjustment is best understood through three interconnected balance sheets: those of households, local governments and the nation.
The household balance sheet is the most important. Official statistics show that 96 per cent of urban households own at least one home and around 45 per cent own two or more. Residential property accounts for roughly 70 per cent of household wealth, compared with about 30 per cent in the United States. Housing therefore functions not merely as shelter but also as retirement savings, collateral, inheritance and long-term financial security.
Chinese households have had few attractive alternatives. Domestic capital markets remain heavily regulated, overseas investment opportunities are limited and the public pension system is relatively modest. Consequently, property became the default savings vehicle, while Hong Kong evolved into the principal channel for overseas investment.
As property values decline, households become more cautious. Precautionary savings rise, discretionary spending weakens and consumer confidence deteriorates. Studies suggest Chinese household consumption is more than twice as sensitive to housing price movements as Japan's during its property correction. Richard Koo's concept of a balance-sheet recession captures this dynamic well: households prioritise repairing their balance sheets over borrowing and spending, regardless of how cheap credit becomes. The problem is confidence rather than the cost of money.
This helps explain why private consumption accounts for only around 40 per cent of GDP, compared with 55–70 per cent in most advanced economies. Investment and exports continue to shoulder a disproportionate share of growth. While exports sustain production and employment, no major economy has achieved durable prosperity without a confident domestic consumer.
The second balance sheet belongs to local governments. For years, land sales financed infrastructure and public services. As property transactions slowed, this revenue contracted sharply. Greater scrutiny of Local Government Financing Vehicles (LGFVs) also revealed substantially larger liabilities than previously recognised, exposing how deeply property had become intertwined with local government finance. Although Beijing retains considerable fiscal flexibility, restoring healthier local government finances remains essential.
The third balance sheet is the national balance sheet. China remains the world's largest manufacturing economy and a global leader in electric vehicles, batteries, renewable energy equipment, industrial robotics and artificial intelligence. These strengths explain why exports have remained resilient. Yet industrial success has not translated into equally robust domestic demand. Domestic vehicle sales have remained broadly stagnant since 2018, manufacturing employment has fallen by around 7.5 million since 2011 as production became increasingly automated, and self-employment has risen from 5–10 per cent of the workforce in 2000 to almost one in three workers today, reflecting the expansion of lower-productivity gig work.
Japan's Lessons—and China's Distinct Path
Comparisons with Japan's Lost Decade are instructive but incomplete. Like Japan, China faces the negative wealth effects of a property correction and an ageing population. Unlike Japan, however, China remains an upper-middle-income economy with considerable scope for productivity gains and technological upgrading. Its banking system is also more insulated from direct property-sector risks, with the principal debtors being developers and LGFVs rather than commercial banks. Combined with substantial state capacity and industrial competitiveness, these factors reduce the likelihood of a Japanese-style financial collapse, even if they do not eliminate the prospect of structurally slower growth.
Confidence Will Define China's Next Development Model
Demographics reinforce the adjustment. China's working-age population is shrinking, fertility rates are among the world's lowest, and only around 6 per cent of Chinese citizens—primarily in Tier One cities—enjoy income levels comparable to Japan's national average. In 2020, one-third of Chinese cities, including several with populations exceeding 10 million, experienced population decline. These trends imply fewer first-time homebuyers, weaker long-term housing demand and stronger incentives for precautionary saving.
China's next phase of development will depend on managing three structural transitions simultaneously: from property-led to productivity-led growth, from investment-driven to consumption-led prosperity, and from demographic dividend to demographic constraint. Achieving these objectives will require deeper capital markets, broader household wealth diversification, stronger retirement security and continued industrial upgrading.
The implications extend far beyond China. As the world's second-largest economy and the largest trading partner for much of Asia, China's rebalancing will reshape commodity markets, regional supply chains, investment flows and global trade.
For four decades, China's economic miracle was powered by investment, urbanisation and industrialisation. The next phase will be judged by a different metric: whether industrial success can be translated into confident households, resilient consumption and sustainable long-term growth. China has already demonstrated that it can build world-class industries. The defining question now is whether it can build a world-class consumer economy. The answer will shape not only China's future, but also the trajectory of the Asian and global economy over the coming decade.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Singapore central bank surprises with policy tightening
Article:
SINGAPORE: Singapore's central bank unexpectedly tightened its monetary policy on Monday.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it would slightly increase the prevailing rate of appreciation of its exchange rate-based policy band, which is known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER).
It said there was no change to the width of the policy band or the level at which it is centred. A majority of analysts polled by Reuters had expected the MAS to hold its policy settings steady.

Title: Succession Planning: Replanting Leadership in Oil Palm
Article:
Oil palm understands time better than most industries. Fruit must be harvested at the right moment. Roads must be maintained before rain turns discipline into drama. Palms must be replanted before ageing yields turn a proud block into a quiet liability.
Yet when it comes to leadership, many plantation organisations still wait too long.
Succession planning in oil palm is not merely a human resource exercise. It is leadership replanting: preparing people who can carry the field book, understand the mill, read the market, engage regulators, reassure investors, speak to workers and smallholders, and steer the business through sustainability and scrutiny.
Plantation leadership was once shaped mainly by field command. That instinct remains vital. No dashboard can replace the experienced eye that knows when the field is telling the truth. But today's leader must also stand where board papers meet muddy boots. The boardroom asks for prudence. Investors ask for confidence. Regulators ask for proof. Workers ask for dignity. Young managers ask whether there is a future worth staying for. The estate asks for decisions before the palms grow old waiting.
That is why succession cannot be accidental. A company does not only need one future managing director. It needs estate managers, mill managers, engineers, agronomists, sustainability officers, finance leaders and public affairs voices who understand how soil, factory, market and society are connected.
Too much institutional wisdom sits in too few heads. Some seniors know which block floods first, which mill weakness will return and which contractor can be trusted. Such knowledge is precious. But when it remains personal rather than institutional, the organisation is exposed.
Poor succession does not always arrive with a loud crisis. More often, it whispers. It appears in assistants who stop asking questions, young managers who see no pathway, supervisors who obey but no longer think, and technical officers who leave because opportunity is clearer elsewhere. Talent is not lost only to competitors. It is also lost to indecision.
Boards must not confuse caution with leadership. Prudence is necessary. But over-applied caution can become inertia wearing a tie. Decisions are deferred. Replanting is slowed. Mechanisation remains a seminar topic. Deputies are named but not empowered.
The estate sees all this. It may not read annual reports, but it reads intent. Workers know when leadership exists only in memos. Young managers know when trust is spoken but not given. Field teams know when sustainability is treated as a department rather than a discipline. Credibility is built more in field conditions than in statements.
Leadership must become translation. It must translate boardroom risk into estate decisions, field realities into boardroom language, regulatory demands into workable systems, and industry frustration into advocacy that is firm, factual and fair. A healthy organisation is one where truth travels upward before damage becomes expensive.
Family-owned companies face an additional test. Succession is also family conversation, legacy and quiet tension. The older generation may see land as sacrifice and identity. The younger generation may see it as capital, burden or an asset requiring professional management. Sometimes, continuity means stewardship through competence, not control by bloodline.
Experience should not be discarded. But if seniors remain too central for too long, succession becomes theatre. The young manager is promoted but still waits for every decision. The board applauds renewal while keeping the old key in the old pocket. That is bonsai leadership: alive, shaped and kept small.
The best seniors do not cling. They coach, open doors and allow younger leaders to decide while remaining available when judgement is needed. Their finest legacy is to make the institution stronger after they step aside.
Boards must treat succession as governance, not gossip over lunch. They should review critical roles, readiness and retention risks. Staff pinching cannot be the industry's main talent strategy; it fills vacancies, but does not grow the sector's bench.
A company that replants palms but not people is only half-prepared for the future. One day, every senior planter must hand over the field book. Every chief executive must leave the boardroom. Every technical guru must pass on knowledge. Every founder must decide whether legacy means control or continuity.
The palms will need harvesting. The mills will still need running. The question is whether someone capable will be walking the rounds across the whole value chain.
Plantations do not reward comfort. They reward stewardship. And stewardship is never a solo act.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Gobind: No automatic sharing of private biometric data [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Private biometric data and building access records collected by smart developments will not be automatically integrated into government systems as Malaysia expands its AI Cities network, Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said.
Addressing privacy concerns, he said the government's push to develop an "AI Nation" was not aimed at creating a mass surveillance system.
Any sharing of personal data, he added, must have a clear legal basis and comply with  data protection laws.
"There are no plans for private biometric information or building access records to be automatically transferred to government systems.
"Any sharing of personal data would require a clear legal basis and compliance with Malaysia's regulations," he told the
New Straits Times.
Gobind said AI-powered city services do not require the centralisation of personal information, as they could operate using aggregated, anonymised or operational data.
His assurance comes amid growing interest in AI-enabled  developments, including I-Bhd's AI Living project at i-City in Shah Alam, which features facial recognition, biometric access and smart CCTV systems in common areas.
To ensure such initiatives  operate within a common national framework, Gobind said the government had established a cross-ministry AI Cities Task Force under the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan (MD2030).
The task force will coordinate standards, governance and system compatibility.
"Our goal is to move beyond standalone and fragmented projects by establishing common foundations that allow AI systems and urban services to operate seamlessly across cities and states."
The task force will develop data-sharing platforms, national data standards, a National AI Algorithm Bank and common AI infrastructure, while allowing private developers to retain ownership and control of their systems.
Gobind said: "The goal is to establish secure standards and systems that enable collaboration where there is clear public or economic value."
He added that commercial independence and privacy obligations would be respected.
He  announced that Malaysia was establishing AI Malaysia to coordinate AI development, alongside a proposed Data Commission to oversee the safe and trusted use of data.
Both initiatives form part of the Malaysia Digital 2030 Action Plan, launched by Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, and are intended to ensure the AI Cities network is built on strong governance and unified standards.
"Ahead of our AI Nation launch on July 28, we are putting institutional foundations, data standards and cross-ministry frameworks in place to ensure AI transformation is cohesive and scalable."
He said the AI Cities initiative was designed to create a connected national ecosystem that would allow cities of all sizes to benefit from shared AI tools and infrastructure.
Gobind added: "This is how we intend to make AI work for the whole nation, not just individual cities."
He added that the government was also drafting the AI Governance Bill to support AI adoption, with public trust remaining central to the initiative's success.
"Malaysians must have confidence that AI is improving their quality of life while protecting their rights, privacy and security."

Title: Japan June services producer prices rise as Iran war keeps freight costs high
Article:
TOKYO: Japan's services producer price index rose 3.2 per cent in June from a year earlier, central bank data showed on Monday, a sign of broadening inflationary pressure that will keep alive market expectations for further interest rate hikes.
The annual rise in the index, which tracks the price companies charge each other for services, followed a revised 3.4 per cent gain in May.
The increase was driven by continued gains in transportation costs, which rose 5.3 per cent in June from a year earlier, as rising fuel prices and supply disruptions from the Middle East conflict kept ocean and air freight charges elevated, the data showed.

Title: AI changes how Malaysians buy products
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian consumers are increasingly deciding what to buy before stepping into a store — with search engines — online reviews and artificial intelligence (AI) tools playing a bigger role in shaping purchasing decisions.
Industry players said the shopping journey is no longer linear, as consumers move between online and offline channels multiple times before making a purchase.
SingleInterface Southeast Asia director Punit Sharma said Malaysia is well positioned to benefit from this shift, supported by its high level of digital adoption and strong small and medium enterprise (SME) ecosystem.
He said Malaysians perform more than 100 million Google searches daily, with about half involving local searches for nearby businesses, products or services.
"Malaysia has a digitally mature consumer base.
"More than 70 per cent of these local searches eventually lead to transactions, highlighting how online discovery increasingly translates into offline sales," he said at the company's official launch in Malaysia recently.
The trend extends beyond retail to sectors, such as banking, healthcare, hospitality and automotive, where customers increasingly use digital platforms to locate nearby branches, compare services and make purchasing decisions.
Despite the opportunities, Punit said many SMEs struggle to manage multiple digital platforms while operating with limited marketing budgets.
Rather than increasing marketing spending, he said SMEs should focus on adopting the right digital tools, with AI helping to automate routine tasks, improve online visibility and generate better returns on investment.
"Many SMEs think these solutions are expensive because they look at the upfront cost. But when you consider the return on investment and the number of functions a single platform can replace, the value becomes much clearer."
SingleInterface recently entered Malaysia through reseller partnerships with Arbell Parc Sdn Bhd and BlackGrid Digital Sdn Bhd, which will provide local consulting, implementation, onboarding, training and customer support to enterprises nationwide.
Founded in India in 2014, SingleInterface serves more than 400 enterprise brands in Asia, including the Middle East.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Corporate demand for AI training doubles, says PEOPLElogy
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping Malaysia's workplaces, with demand for AI-related corporate training doubling this year as businesses race to equip employees with new skills.
PEOPLElogy Bhd founder and managing director Allen Lee said organisations are increasingly investing in practical AI training as it becomes more deeply embedded in the workplace.
Beyond boosting productivity, the technology is now capable of automating complex tasks, analysing vast amounts of information and transforming entire job functions.
"We have seen a 100 per cent increase in demand for AI-related training programmes this year," he told Business Times in an interview.
The strongest demand comes from companies seeking to train employees on widely used generative AI platforms such as ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Claude.
Rather than using AI solely to generate content, organisations are increasingly applying the technology to automate workflows, process information and support decision-making.
"If you get humans to analyse, it will take some time. But if you ask AI to do analysis, they will not stop. They will not go for coffee. They will just actually immediately do the analysis for you," he said.
Lee expects occupations such as accountants, finance personnel, administrative staff, marketers and operations employees to undergo significant transformation as AI adoption accelerates.
AI Is More Than Just Another Tool
Despite the growing adoption, Lee said many people still underestimate AI's capabilities.
He said AI is often viewed alongside software such as Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint, when in reality it is increasingly capable of performing analytical work and automating tasks traditionally carried out by humans.
"People always mistake AI as just another tool to work on their tasks, like Word, Excel or PowerPoint. But as a matter of fact, it is far more powerful than that."
He also dismissed the common perception that AI will affect only white-collar workers.
"In fact, AI, generally people thought that it's only replacing all the white-collar jobs. But it's not just as simple as white-collar job. It can actually replace anybody's job.
"As long as the company, the individual has to do automation, analysis, all these things, AI will actually take over."
Workers Must Adapt
Lee believes the bigger question is no longer whether AI will change jobs, but whether workers are prepared for the transition.
He cited estimates from the Human Resources Ministry and TalentCorp that nearly 700,000 jobs in Malaysia could eventually be affected by AI and digitalisation.
Rather than viewing AI as a threat, he said workers should focus on building capabilities that complement the technology.
Lee identified four key priorities: proficiency in generative AI, data literacy, critical thinking and adaptability.
"People need to be very data literate. That means they have to be very sensitive with data and human-centric soft skill like critical thinking," he said.
"But more importantly is adaptability. The biggest challenge for every individual is embracing change. If they don't adapt to the environment, ultimately they will be replaced."
He added that learning AI does not necessarily require technical expertise.
"We need to let people see how easy it is to adopt AI. Once they experience how much more productive they can become, they will naturally follow."
Change Remains the Biggest Challenge
Despite growing interest in AI, Lee said organisational resistance to change remains the biggest hurdle to wider adoption.
"I guess typically like any individual or organisation, embracing change is always the most challenging one."
To help address this, PEOPLElogy launched the "I Am AI Ready" movement, which aims to reach five million Malaysians over the next 36 months through awareness campaigns, assessments, certification programmes and industry collaborations.
The initiative brings together universities, government ministries, non-governmental organisations, technology partners, corporations and community groups to educate Malaysians about AI and assess their readiness.
Lee said universities are a key focus because many students still have limited exposure to practical AI programmes.
"We are reaching out to hundreds of thousands of students about the importance of AI," he said.
PEOPLElogy has also signed memorandums of understanding with JSkill, PIKOM, Century Software and the Malaysia Retail Chain Association, while collaborating with Infoline IT Solutions, FWD Malaysia Holdings, Taylor's College and Multimedia University to support AI training and ecosystem development.
The initiative also targets small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which Lee believes stand to benefit significantly from AI despite often lacking specialised talent.
"The biggest challenge for SMEs is talent, and by leveraging on AI, it can reduce the dependability on just talent, or maybe they can actually just get all the talents to learn more AI," he said.
Malaysia's AI Ambitions
Malaysia aims to become an AI-driven economy by 2030, but Lee believes success will depend as much on mindset as on technology.
"I'm sure AI is moving very fast and people need to adapt. People need to be flexible on all the policy making," he said.
He added that data protection will become increasingly important as AI adoption expands.
"There are many people that are reluctant to change. The only thing that we can educate them is if you don't change, the world will change them already."

Title: Malaysia stands out as global firms diversify supply chains
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is well positioned to benefit from the ongoing diversification of global supply chains, supported by its mature industrial ecosystem, skilled workforce and strategic location, according to Citi's top executive.
Citi Asia South head Amol Gupte said companies are redesigning their supply chains to make them more resilient, with production and sourcing spread across multiple markets instead of being concentrated in a single country.
"What we're seeing today is companies redesigning supply chains to be more diversified, resilient and geographically distributed.
"Supply chains have been reconfigured, and companies now have multiple production and sourcing bases.
"This is not a winner-takes-all story within Asia. Several markets in the region have become key intermediary hubs as companies balance efficiency, resilience and access to growth markets," he told Business Times.
Gupte said Malaysia has secured an attractive position in this evolving landscape, particularly in electronics and advanced manufacturing.
"In that context, Malaysia occupies an attractive position. It has built a sophisticated industrial base, particularly in electronics and advanced manufacturing, over decades.
"Malaysia combines industrial depth, talent, connectivity, natural resources, a regulatory environment valued by global investors, and a strategic location at the heart of Southeast Asia," he said.
He highlighted Penang as one of the region's most established semiconductor and electronics hubs, with a technology and manufacturing ecosystem developed over several decades.
Looking ahead, Gupte said many of the global investment themes emerging today align closely with Malaysia's strengths.
"The rapid growth of AI is driving demand for semiconductors, servers, power systems and advanced electronics, reinforcing Malaysia's established strengths in the electrical and electronics (E&E) and semiconductor sectors," he said.
He added that Malaysia already possesses many of the qualities sought by global investors, including a strong industrial base, skilled talent, robust infrastructure and a clear strategic focus on technology and digital growth.
Beyond semiconductors and advanced electronics, Gupte identified digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) as sectors with the strongest long-term growth prospects.
He said AI continues to fuel demand for data centres, cloud infrastructure, semiconductors, servers and power systems, following significant investments by several of the world's leading hyperscalers.
Other sectors with strong potential include education, healthcare, aerospace maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO), pharmaceuticals, biopharma, advanced manufacturing and high-performance materials.
On AI-related investments, Gupte said the technology is driving a structural capital expenditure cycle that will support demand across the wider technology and industrial ecosystem.
"The growth of AI is fuelling a structural capital expenditure cycle, which will continue to drive demand across semiconductors, energy systems, industrial equipment and the broader digital ecosystem," he said.
He added that Malaysia is well positioned within the AI ecosystem, having built its capabilities over decades and established a more than 50-year track record in electronics and semiconductors that remains foundational to the AI value chain.
Gupte also sees significant opportunities for Malaysian companies across Asean, which is projected to become the world's fourth-largest economy by 2030.
"There are opportunities for companies that view Asean as a platform for regional expansion, not merely an export market," he said.
He added that stronger connectivity between Asean and China is creating opportunities across manufacturing, technology, green industries and the digital economy.
On Malaysia's financial sector, Gupte said the country remains a key destination for foreign direct investment from the United States, Europe and across Asia, while Malaysian companies continue to tap global capital markets to fund expansion.
He said Citi is supporting multinational companies expanding in Malaysia, including a global surgical robotics company establishing a regional manufacturing hub in Penang and leading semiconductor firms from the US and Taiwan building advanced facilities in the state.
"These are tangible examples of high-quality capital and technology flowing into the country, and they require a sophisticated financial ecosystem to support them. Our role is to provide that," he said.

Title: Iran halts strikes as Trump gives space to talks
Article:
TEHERAN: Iran and the United States held their fire Sunday, handing Gulf shipping and the oil industry a respite from missile strikes as Donald Trump's UN envoy said the president was "giving talks some space."
Iran said it had halted retaliatory attacks against Washington's allies in the Middle East, and US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told "Fox News Sunday" that, while forces remained "locked and loaded", Trump would give negotiations "a little bit of room."
Prior to Friday, the US military had carried out strikes on Iran for 13 consecutive nights, in the largest rekindling of the almost five-month-old war since an April ceasefire. But two consecutive nights have now passed without bombing.
"These attacks continued until two nights ago, but over the past two nights the Americans have stopped their attacks," said Iran's army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia. "Since... our strategy has essentially been retaliatory, we have also halted our retaliatory operations."
Fighting over the strategic Strait of Hormuz derailed diplomatic efforts between Washington and Tehran, but the conflict then expanded beyond the vital energy corridor to include attacks on US bases, regional shipping and Gulf allies.
Unconfirmed Iranian media reports on Sunday said an oil tanker had been damaged by a sea mine.
'ONE WAY OR THE OTHER'
The recent lull has revived hopes of a return to negotiations, although American media reported the pause could also reflect pressure on US stockpiles of Patriot interceptors and other defensive weapons.
Waltz dismissed this idea, in a second interview with NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"I want to be crystal clear. The US military – and I've verified this every which way – has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be," he insisted.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due at the White House on Tuesday, and is expected to urge Trump to continue to take a tough line on Tehran, in particular on its nuclear programme.
Iran has long insisted the programme is for civilian purposes but which the US and its allies allege is aimed at developing a weapon.
Also speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said he fully backed Trump's efforts to shut down Iran's nuclear programme.
"If he can do so without returning to intense military fighting, that's fine. Why not? But one way or the other, they have to end their nuclear programme, and with a deal or without a deal, that has to come to an end," he said.
Plans to escalate the US campaign have been shelved in part because of shrinking munitions supplies, The New York Times reported, citing two people briefed on the matter.
NEW FRONT
Trump also faces the risk of a wider Middle East war, the estrangement of vulnerable Gulf allies and further shocks to the global economy, the newspaper said.
Trump said on Friday he had not decided whether to return to an all-out operation.
"We're talking to them right now. I think they're getting more and more serious," he told journalists.
The war that Trump once predicted would last four or five weeks is now nearing its fifth month, and is weighing on the Republican's approval ratings ahead of crucial US midterm elections in November.
On Sunday locals in Tehran carried on with a normal morning, dealing with heavy traffic jams on their way to work, an AFP journalist said.
Shops and restaurants were open as usual as the city suffered a heatwave.
Fighting has meanwhile spread to a new front.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Sunday said they downed a Saudi drone over northwestern Yemen, a day after the Yemeni group claimed it attacked oil facilities in the Gulf kingdom.
The Houthis had said they struck Saudi Aramco sites in Jizan and Yanbu, after Riyadh bombed Houthi targets on Friday.

Title: Shein flags tariff hits after posting quarterly loss ahead of Hong Kong IPO
Article:
SINGAPORE/BEIJING: Shein swung to a US$99 million quarterly loss due to slowing sales after the US removed an import duty exemption on small packages and a hefty one-time accounting charge, the online retailer's pre-IPO financial filings showed on Sunday.
The filing, which lays the groundwork for investor roadshows and official bookbuilding of its much-awaited Hong Kong IPO, showed that Shein posted a loss in the first quarter of 2026 compared with a net income of US$395 million a year earlier.
The European Union, a key market for Shein, also this month imposed a €3 fee on low-value e-commerce imports, to curb what the EU calls unfair competition from China.
The Singapore-headquartered company, which was founded in China, did not disclose the size of the Hong Kong share sale, the offer price, the listing timetable, or expected proceeds from the offering in the draft prospectus.
Shein won approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) for its Hong Kong listing on July 10, clearing the way for a listing after failed attempts in New York and London.
UNDER PRESSURE
The financial details give investors a sharper look at the pressure facing Shein as it seeks new funds amid higher costs, slower growth, and growing regulatory scrutiny in key markets.
The first-quarter loss partly reflected an accounting change under which it took a US$328 million fair-value charge on convertible redeemable preferred shares. These are investor shares that can later convert into ordinary shares, and their accounting value can change before a listing.
The accounting loss comes as Shein, which sells US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans in around 160 countries, saw a sharp drop in its valuation in recent years as a pandemic-driven online shopping boom faded and the U.S. closed the "de ⁠minimis" duty loophole.
Shein was seeking a valuation of US$40 to US$50 billion in its IPO, Reuters reported this month, citing a source with knowledge of the matter. That's a far cry from the US$100 billion value that media reported it was given in a funding round in 2022.
'DE MINIMIS' REMOVAL
Since May 2025, the removal of the de minimis exemption has had an "adverse impact" on sales in the US, Shein's biggest market, and on overall growth, and has contributed to an increase in expenses, the company said in the filing.
The de minimis rule had allowed packages worth less than $800 to enter the US without duties. Shein said Chinese-origin products sold by it or through its marketplace and shipped to the US are now subject to tax rates ranging from 10 per cent to 87.5 per cent.
"In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," it said.
Shein's US revenue fell 14.3 per cent to US$2.04 billion in the first quarter from US$2.38 billion a year earlier. The US accounted for 22.5 per cent of quarterly revenue, down from 29.4 per cent of annual revenue in 2023.
Europe accounted for about one-third of Shein's revenues in 2025 and could also be affected this year by the EU duty.
"Although it remains too early to fully assess, it is possible that trends in the EU could be generally in line with or exceed the impact observed in the US after the removal of the US de minimis exemption," Shein warned in the prospectus.
For the entire business, the company's 2025 net income fell 38.7 per cent to US$2.06 billion from the preceding year, while revenues grew 8 per cent to US$41.85 billion, slowing from 20.7 per cent growth in 2024, the filing showed.
Its operating margin dropped to 2.9 per cent in the first quarter from 3.9 per cent in the year-ago period.
REGULATORY CHALLENGES
Founded in Nanjing, Shein has found itself at the centre of growing trade tensions between the US and China.
It has faced criticism from rivals, regulators and advocacy groups over issues including working conditions in supplier factories, allegedly addictive features of its shopping app, and the environmental impact of shipping large volumes by air.
Shein has said it has a zero-tolerance policy on labour abuses, and has invested in risk assessments and mitigation frameworks to safeguard users.
In the prospectus, Shein said the majority of products manufactured by its supply chain partners are stored in central warehouses in China before shipping. In 2025, products stored in Chinese central warehouses accounted for more than 90 per cent of net revenue.
The company said its IPO proceeds would be used to improve technology, raise brand awareness, expand its global presence, promote corporate responsibility and for general corporate purposes.
Shein's pre-IPO investors included IDG, Sequoia Capital, HongShan, Tiger Global, Boyu, Brookfield and General Atlantic, among others, the draft prospectus showed.
The filing listed founder Sky Yangtian Xu, who founded the company in 2012, as chairman and chief executive. Donald Tang, who had served as executive chairman, was not listed among Shein's directors or senior management.
Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley and JPMorgan are joint sponsors of the listing, the filing showed.

Title: PJ food court traders choose flood risk over relocation
Article:
PETALING JAYA: Traders at Medan Selera 223 in Seksyen 51A here have decided to stay put despite being warned that they  face flood risks during a six-month mitigation project.
The traders said they welcomed the construction of a flood retention pond next to the food court, but were unwilling to move as it was unclear whether it would be temporary or permanent.
Medan Selera PJ Lestari Traders Association chairman Farahanim Ahmad, 43, said mayor Datuk Mohamad Zahri Samingon had given traders the option of  relocating during construction.
"If the Petaling Jaya City Council  asks us to move temporarily, upgrades the food court and then  lets us return, I would gladly do it. But  traders here have decided to stay put," she said.
Farahanim said traders were told their stalls would not be affected and business could continue as usual.
However, traders had also been told that if flooding occurred during the pond's construction, they would have to bear the risk themselves, she added.
"The main parking lot will be closed for six months during construction, so customers will need to park along the road.
"But the city council has promised that access to the food court will stay open."
She said the food court had 60 lots, of which only 40 were  operating, and business had dropped by about 70 per cent following repeated floods.
"Customers are afraid to come here because of the floods. We hope this will be resolved."
Traders at the food court endured their fourth flash flood this year on July 18 and have sought answers from the authorities on long-term measures to prevent further flooding.
State Infrastructure and Agriculture Committee chairman Datuk Izham Hashim previously said an on-site flood retention pond would be built near Medan Selera 223 to  store excess water during flash floods.
The RM4.55 million project is expected to be completed by year end.
Farahanim thanked Zahri, the city council and the state government for acting swiftly following the floods.
"Floods are natural disasters, but the authorities came quickly, listened to us and pushed for a real solution. That gives us a lot of reassurance."
Third-generation trader Mardiantynur Marhisham, 41, said traders were prepared to accept the risks during construction because they did not want to leave the area.
She said Zahri had visited the site on Friday to brief traders on the planned works and asked whether they wanted to relocate or stay.
"But they didn't specify whether relocating meant temporarily for the construction or permanently. Either way, most of us refused to move.
"They told us that if we stayed while the project was ongoing over the next six months, any flooding would be at our own risk. We accepted that.
"We are  willing to take that risk during construction because we love this location and refuse to leave."
Mardiantynur said the area had experienced severe flooding in April, May and July.
"The worst part was having barely 15 minutes after we  heard the siren  to pack up before the water rose and ruined our freezers and belongings.
"Knowing there is finally a solution from the government and city council gives us huge relief for next year."
On Thursday, the state government allocated RM40.5 million for immediate and medium-term flood mitigation projects at
hotspots under the Petaling Jaya City Council's jurisdiction.
Izham said the plan included 39 projects to strengthen flood defences in high-risk areas, including Section 51A, Kampung Cempaka and Jalan Kuala Selangor.
To ease the traders' burden, the city council has also granted a one-month rental exemption and a 30 per cent rental discount until December.
The council has also installed flood sensors and warning sirens along Jalan 223 and is upgrading the system to provide earlier alerts of up to 30 minutes.

Title: Malaysia's agarwood industry gathers steam
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's efforts to develop a high-value agarwood industry are gaining steam, with private sector players expanding production and commercial cultivation months after the government identified the commodity as a promising new growth area.
The latest move comes from Agartech Ventures Sdn Bhd, which plans to nearly double annual production of its hybrid agarwood seedlings to one million as it seeks to position Malaysia as a regional hub for agarwood chips and premium gaharu products.
In February, plantation and commodities minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia has significant untapped potential in the agarwood industry, which he estimated to be worth about US$1 billion globally.
He called for greater commercial cultivation using sustainable planting and management practices instead of harvesting wild agarwood from forests, as part of efforts to develop higher value-added products.
Agartech chairman Datuk Hishamuddin Abdul Karim said the company currently produces about 600,000 MyKynam hybrid agarwood seedlings annually from two nurseries spanning 5.26 hectares in Lendu, Melaka.
To support its expansion, the company plans to establish a joint venture in Perlis that will serve as its northern production hub to meet growing domestic and international demand.
He said one acre of land could accommodate about 2,000 agarwood trees, with each tree valued at around RM75.
Hishamuddin also highlighted the industry's downstream value, saying one litre of extracted agarwood oil could fetch up to RM60,000.
He said the broader industry could be worth as much as US$12 billion annually, reflecting demand across premium wood chips, essential oils, perfumes, pharmaceuticals and other agarwood-based products.
The company's expansion follows nearly a decade of research and development (R&D), which has resulted in 24 hybrid agarwood varieties since 2017, including MyKynam, a cross between the Aquilaria malaccensis species and China's Kynam agarwood.
Hishamuddin said MyKynam produces premium organic resin and heartwood that have attracted buyers from China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, the Middle East and Europe.
"Malaysia has all the ingredients to emerge as a global leader in the agarwood industry, including a suitable tropical climate, fertile land, rich biodiversity, strong logistics infrastructure, advanced R&D capabilities and skilled talent," he said during a luncheon with the media recently.
However, he said the industry's growth would require coordinated support from the government, industry players, private investors, research institutions, academia and the media.
Hishamuddin said the Malaysian Timber Industry Board has an important role in industry capacity building, technical support, standards development and market expansion.
Meanwhile, Universiti Agrosains Malaysia in Melaka is a strategic partner in R&D, innovation and talent development.
He said Agartech Ventures was established to develop the MyKynam industry through scientific research, hybrid seed development, commercial plantation expansion and human capital development.
Following the completion of its R&D phase, the company is now shifting its focus towards building a broader industry ecosystem through strategic collaborations in technology transfer, capacity building, investment and market development.
As part of the initiative, Agartech has introduced its Agartech Vision 2035, a long-term strategy that includes expanding nursery and commercial plantation networks, empowering local entrepreneurs and smallholders, strengthening innovation and widening export markets.
Hishamuddin said the company aims to ensure the industry creates value beyond corporate profits by generating employment, increasing rural incomes and contributing to the country's economic growth.
He also described the media as a strategic partner in raising public awareness and investor confidence, saying accurate and balanced reporting would help unlock the industry's full potential and support the development of another high-value agricultural sector in Malaysia.

Title: Malaysia gains tariff edge over Asean rivals
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's 10 per cent US tariff has left its exporters in a stronger competitive position than many regional peers, although the advantage may prove temporary unless the country follows through on promised trade reforms.
Kenanga Research head Peter Kong said the focus on Malaysia retaining the 10 per cent tariff has overshadowed a more significant development: regional competitors including Thailand, Vietnam, Singapore and the Philippines now face higher tariffs of 12.5 per cent.
"The United States did not lower Malaysia's tariffs. It raised everyone else's," Kong told Business Times.
Malaysia's 10 per cent tariff remains unchanged from the temporary rate that expired on July 24, meaning the immediate cost for most exporters stays broadly the same.
Kong said the final tariff schedule gives Malaysia a 2.5 percentage point advantage over several Asean competitors in the US market, particularly in electrical and electronics, electronics manufacturing services, rubber products and processed food.
He said the difference may appear modest, but could influence sourcing decisions in industries where margins are thin and supply chains are highly competitive.
"The tariff itself has barely changed. Malaysia's competitive position has," he said.
Besides Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia also remain in the 10 per cent tariff tier.
Kong also clarified that the US Trade Representative's (USTR) findings should not be interpreted as evidence that Malaysian exports are produced using forced labour.
Instead, the investigation found that Malaysia lacks a legal mechanism to prevent imports of goods produced with forced labour in third countries from entering domestic supply chains before being re-exported.
"This is a regulatory finding, not a judgment on Malaysian manufacturers," he said.
Kong noted that the final tariff schedule also retained product-specific exemptions for palm oil, tropical wood and plywood.
Malaysia is also one of only four economies, alongside Bangladesh, Cambodia and Indonesia, to receive textile quotas.
The quotas allow a specified volume of apparel exports to enter the US free of the new tariff, subject to purchases of American cotton and textile inputs.
However, Kong cautioned that the current tariff advantage is not guaranteed.
"This does not mean the risk has gone. Tariff rates remain open to future review. The current outcome is an opportunity, not a permanent advantage," he said.
He added that Malaysia's longer-term competitiveness will depend on how quickly it fulfils commitments made under the reciprocal trade framework.
The Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry has established an inter-agency task force and begun reviewing the Customs Act 1967 to strengthen Malaysia's forced labour import controls, although legislative amendments have yet to be passed.
"The real policy challenge is not today's decision. It is keeping Malaysia's edge before the next review," Kong said.
"In trade, competitiveness rests not only on the tariff imposed on you, but also on the tariff imposed on everyone else. On that measure, Malaysia's position looks stronger today than the headlines suggest, though the edge is thin and not yet secured."
Separately, Kenanga Research said Taiwan's placement in the same tariff tier limits the likelihood of significant shifts in semiconductor supply chains.
"As a result, investor attention is likely to focus more on product-level exposure, exclusion eligibility and the sustainability of Malaysia's tariff classification than on country-level designation alone," it said in a note.
The research house also does not expect the latest tariff decision to materially alter Malaysia's broader macroeconomic outlook.
It maintained its forecast for Malaysia's gross domestic product (GDP) growth at the upper end of its 4.5 per cent to 5.0 per cent range in 2026, compared with 5.2 per cent in 2025.
"This is supported by continued resilience in external demand, with exports forecast to grow 9.7 per cent in 2026, alongside a still healthy current account surplus of 2.1 per cent of GDP.
"From a policy perspective, Malaysia's ongoing engagement with the USTR and efforts to establish an import prohibition framework for goods produced with forced labour in third countries provide an avenue to address the regulatory gap identified under the Section 301 investigation," it added.
On Friday, the government said Malaysia's placement in the lower tariff tier reflected the USTR's recognition of the country's commitment to implement and enforce laws prohibiting the importation of goods produced using forced labour.
It added that the USTR's Section 301 investigation into excess capacity involving 16 economies, including Malaysia, remains ongoing.

Title: Citrawarna 2026 showcases Malaysia's culture to global audiences
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  Citrawarna 2026 drew more than 700 visitors from 12 countries, with international guests experiencing one of Malaysia's biggest cultural showcases under Visit Malaysia 2026.
Visitors from China, India, Mauritius, Japan, Vietnam, Indonesia, Singapore, Kazakhstan, Italy, the Netherlands, Switzerland and France attended Saturday's opening through curated travel packages.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim launched the annual  showcase at Dataran Merdeka here.
The three-day event is featuring 3,500 performers representing states, three federal territories and the  multicultural communities in its signature Colours of Parade (
Citra Perarakan
).
The festival started  with an opening performance, followed by the parade and a post-show performance watched by spectators along Jalan Raja and at the Sultan Abdul Samad Building.
[[nid:1497733]]
Present was Tourism, Arts and Culture Minister Datuk Seri Tiong King Sing.
Citrawarna  features four signature experiences: Colours of Parade, Colours of Flavour, Colours of Culture and Colours of Art.
The event includes more than 70 food and beverage offerings, over 20 cultural activity stations, and more than 10 arts and crafts booths.
Visitors were also invited to participate in hands-on activities, including batik painting, ketupat weaving and traditional culinary demonstrations led by artisans and cultural practitioners.
Highlights included  performances by  Wani Kayrie, Bulan Asryaff, Dr Soo Wincci, Santesh Kumar, Ernie Zakri, Aina Abdul and Kumpulan Balle-Balle.
Themed
Ritma Warisan, Nadi Nusa dan Bangsa
, this year's edition highlights Malaysia's rich  heritage.

Title: Students find alternative paths after missing out on public university places
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:   Missing out on a public university placement is not the end of the road, as scholarships and a wide range of higher education options are available at other institutions.
Aishah Ahmad Firdaus, 24, from Shah Alam, was devastated after failing to secure a pre-university place through UPUOnline — the portal to apply for courses in public universities. She later secured a scholarship to pursue a  degree in psychology at a private university.
Looking back, Aishah said she wished  school leavers  had received   guidance on completing their UPU applications instead of relying  on word of mouth.
"There wasn't any crash course on UPU. We just did it ourselves or asked friends about it," she told the
New Straits Times.
Although she was advised to diversify her programme choices, Aishah said she did not cast her net wide enough.
After her  unsuccessful application, Aishah said she was reluctant to consider private higher education because of the financial burden on her parents.
"I remember researching university rankings and graduate outcomes because I wanted reassurances that I could still build a good future.
"Ironically, choosing that path became one of the biggest turning points in my life," she said.
Aishah now works as a journey design architect in the banking sector, applying her psychology background to improve customer experiences.
Meanwhile, associate creative director Fahrul Fahlevi Fuad, 32, from Shah Alam, said he pursued higher education at a private university after missing out on a public university placement, thanks to his family's support.
"I was all right with it because I knew my parents could afford to send me to a private university. I also knew there were others who needed public university places more," he said.
Fahrul said he knew of options such as Mara colleges and other private institutions, but his family ultimately chose a university based on its reputation and graduate employability.
He said he had always been drawn to the intersection of technology and creativity, and wanted to help organisations accelerate their digital transformation.
Now designing digital products and user experiences for organisations in Southeast Asia, Fahrul believes success depends more on attitude than where  students studied.
"What matters is your intention, your curiosity and your dedication to grow wherever you end up," he said.

Title: 12 policemen nabbed after Vanuatu citizen claims RM2 million extortion bid [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Twelve policemen  have been arrested for allegedly extorting RM2 million from a Vanuatu citizen.
Sources said the victim had paid  US$140,000 (RM560,000) to the suspects.
The victim  lodged a report at the Dang Wangi district police headquarters, prompting an  investigation.
It is understood that those arrested included  deputy superintendents and assistant superintendents, as well as rank-and-file personnel.
Sources said the group had allegedly demanded RM2 million from the victim, but he paid  only RM560,000 before lodging a report. Investigators have also recovered part of the money  linked to the case.
Dang Wangi police chief Assistant Commissioner Sazalee Adam confirmed the arrests.
The case is similar to an  incident in February,  when a group of  China nationals alleged policemen   robbed them of 50,000 units of the  in Tether cryptocurrency in Kajang.
A lawyer  representing the Chinese nationals   has questioned the delay in investigations.
The lawyer, identified as Charles, said 12 policemen were identified as the suspects, but   no charges had been brought against them.
The case drew public attention after eight Chinese nationals claimed they were forced to transfer 50,000 units of the Tether stablecoin cryptocurrency after police raided a rented bungalow in Country Heights, Kajang, on suspicion that scam-related activities were taking place there.
Those detained comprised an assistant superintendent, an inspector, a sergeant, six corporals, two lance corporals and a constable, aged between 24 and 47.
The arrests followed a report lodged by a Chinese market surveyor, who claimed he and seven friends were forced to transfer cryptocurrency to secure their release.
Police, however, found no evidence  linked to any scam.
The group told police they were market surveyors employed by a China-based company.
The victims alleged they were threatened with arrest and immigration action unless they paid RM400,000.
Fearing for their safety, particularly as three women were among them, one of the victims contacted his employer in China.
After negotiations, the suspects agreed to accept 50,000 units of the Tether cryptocurrency, which was transferred to a wallet address  provided by the suspects.
Charles said technical and digital forensic reports in such cases   usually took  between one and two months to complete.
"Why is this taking so long? Technical reports do not usually take forever."
He said last week, police told him they had identified a Chinese Malaysian  who owned the crypto account where the money was transferred to on Feb 5.
He urged authorities not to delay charging the 12 policemen implicated in the case simply because investigators are still pursuing the wanted man.

Title: Unequal access leaves students behind in varsity race
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR:  The public university admission system is structured and transparent, but unequal access to information, guidance and opportunities can leave some school leavers at a disadvantage.
Visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute Ooi Kok Hin said UPUOnline, the central  public university admission portal,  has clear  criteria, but  students' chances of securing places are often shaped long before they submit their applications, including by their pre-university pathways and access to guidance.
He said students from different backgrounds do not enjoy the same access to application strategies, scholarship opportunities and course selection advice, creating what he described as a "hidden curriculum".
"Some schools, especially boarding schools and certain urban schools, conduct workshops to teach students how to apply for pre-university programmes, scholarships and even how to strategise their choices.
"But for some students, especially those whose parents never had tertiary education, this information is  not as accessible," he told the
New Straits Times
.
Ooi  said while the Internet has improved access to information, it has not levelled the playing field, especially for rural and low-income students who may not know where to find  guidance.
PhD candidate in sociology of education Shakira Teh Sharifuddin said competition for university places varies according to course demand and institutional reputation.
She said sought-after courses such as medicine, engineering, accounting and economics are  more competitive because of stronger demand.
"Certain courses and institutions are more competitive because of factors such as reputation, location and access to information," she said.
Shakira said students' chances are also influenced by academic qualifications, co-curricular achievements, their understanding of the Physical, Sports and Co-curricular Assessment,  as well as access to counselling and career guidance.
She said limited exposure could also prevent students from considering related fields within their areas of interest.
"Someone interested in medicine may not know about related fields such as pharmacy, pharmacology or bioscience because of a lack of information and exposure," she said.
Ooi said debate over the UPU system often centres on degree admissions, where competition between students from different pre-university pathways, including Sijil Tinggi Persekolahan Malaysia  and matriculation, remains a longstanding concern.
He said students who failed to secure places in public universities after completing these pathways have few affordable alternatives unless they opt for polytechnics or state universities.
Ooi said improving fairness requires more than reviewing admission criteria, as equal access to information and guidance is equally important.
Meanwhile, UPU said applicants who were unsuccessful or receive only certificate-level offers may submit appeals within the stipulated period.
Applicants who remain unsuccessful after the appeal  may still pursue higher education through second-intake programmes  or by reapplying through UPUOnline for the 2027/2028  session.
